questions.question:
D6 — What shape is the backoff curve: jitter and a maximum delay, or raw exponential?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md retry framework, finding F6 (PLAN.md:6-8); R1 and R4 fixed.
ELI10: Exponential backoff doubles the wait each attempt: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s. Two problems with the raw version. First, if 500 jobs fail at the same moment because a downstream API blipped, they all retry at exactly the same moments too, which re-creates the spike. Jitter adds randomness so they spread out. Second, without a ceiling, attempt 8 is minutes away and attempt 12 is hours; a cap (say 5 minutes) keeps the tail sane.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a 30-second outage turns into repeated self-inflicted spikes, and users wait far longer than needed for late attempts.
Recommendation: A because both additions are a few lines in the shared backoff function and they are the two things every source on retry design agrees on.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Net: three-line curve that behaves under load vs the textbook curve that misbehaves in exactly the scenario retries exist for.

❌ Jitter makes exact delays non-deterministic; tests must inject the random source

❌ Every job that failed together retries together; retry storms remain possible

❌ Lockstep retries and an unbounded tail; attempt 5 at base 1s is 16s but base 5s is 80s and climbing

D5 — R2: Add jitter to the backoff curve?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md retry framework, `backoff()` function approved in D4.
ELI10: If 500 jobs fail together when a downstream API blips, a plain exponential curve makes all 500 retry at exactly the same second, then again at 2s, 4s, 8s. That synchronized wave ("thundering herd") can knock the API over again. Jitter multiplies each delay by a random factor so the retries spread out. PLAN.md mentions no jitter.
Stakes if we pick wrong: without jitter, a recovering dependency gets hit by the full retry wave at once and the outage repeats on a schedule; with jitter, individual retry timing becomes non-deterministic (tests must inject the RNG).
Recommendation: A because full jitter is the documented industry default (AWS, resilience4j) and costs one injected random() call.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10

options.description:
✅ Spreads a batch of simultaneous failures across the whole delay window, protecting the recovering dependency
✅ Still one pure function; tests pass a fixed RNG and assert the bounds (human: ~2h / CC: ~5 min)
❌ Individual job wait time is no longer predictable from the attempt number alone

Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md:16-18 rewrites `processWebhookJob()`, today at-most-once.

✅ Persisted delivered marker checked before each attempt means a timed-out-but-received send is not re-sent after the marker lands
❌ Contract change for receivers must be documented; a receiver that ignores the header can still see a duplicate in the timeout window

D5 — Should the backoff curve include jitter?
Project/branch/task: branch main, PLAN.md:6-8 wants a custom exponential curve but never says whether delays are randomized.
ELI10: If 500 jobs fail together because a downstream service blipped, plain exponential backoff has all 500 retry at the exact same moments (1s, 2s, 4s...), hitting the recovering service in waves. Jitter picks a random delay between 0 and the exponential ceiling so the retries spread out. It is a one-line change inside computeBackoff() and makes the curve non-deterministic, so tests inject the random source.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without jitter a downstream outage can be prolonged by your own retry storms. With jitter the only cost is a seeded random in tests.
Recommendation: A because full jitter is the documented best practice (AWS, Google) and costs one line plus an injectable RNG. Effort: A (human: ~1 h / CC: ~3 min), B (human: 0 / CC: 0).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Net: spread-out retries vs. a deterministic curve that is easier to eyeball but stampedes.

options.label: Full jitter (recommended)
options.description: ✅ delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)); retries from a mass failure spread evenly instead of arriving in synchronized waves. ✅ Tests pass an injected RNG so assertions stay deterministic. ❌ Individual delays are no longer predictable from the attempt number alone when reading logs.

options.label: No jitter, pure exponential
options.description: ✅ Delay is a pure function of attempt number; trivially readable in logs and tests. ✅ Zero extra code. ❌ Synchronized retry waves after any shared downstream failure; the classic thundering-herd pitfall.

questions.question:
D6 — What is the maximum single backoff delay (the cap)?
Project/branch/task: branch main, PLAN.md:6-8 curve has no stated base or ceiling.
ELI10: Exponential growth gets silly fast: with a 1-second base, attempt 12 waits over an hour and attempt 20 waits 12 days. A cap says "never wait longer than X between attempts" so a long outage is retried at a steady rhythm instead of one attempt per week. The cap also bounds how long a job can be 'in retry' once you multiply it by max attempts (next question).
Stakes if we pick wrong: Too low a cap keeps hammering a downed service; too high (or none) means a webhook event from a 20-minute outage might not be redelivered for hours.
Recommendation: A because 1 s base / 5 min cap recovers from typical outages within minutes and, with a modest attempt count, bounds total retry time to under an hour. Effort is identical across options (one constant).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=10/10, C=3/10
Net: minutes-scale redelivery vs. hours-scale vs. unbounded.

options.label: Base 1 s, cap 5 min (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Ceiling sequence 1s,2s,4s...256s,300s: recovers from short blips in seconds and steady-states at 5 min for longer outages. ✅ Total retry window stays under an hour for ~10 attempts, easy to reason about in alerts. ❌ A multi-hour downstream outage exhausts attempts and dead-letters; needs a replay path (covered by R7).

options.label: Base 1 s, cap 1 h
options.description: ✅ Survives long downstream outages with fewer attempts before dead-letter. ✅ Fewer wasted calls during a prolonged outage. ❌ Webhook consumers may wait an hour between redelivery attempts; time-sensitive events arrive late.

options.label: No cap, pure exponential
options.description: ✅ Simplest formula; nothing to tune. ✅ Matches the plan as written ("same shape as the library version"). ❌ Attempt 12+ waits hours to days; a job can sit in retry effectively forever.

questions.question:
D7 — How many attempts before a job is dead-lettered, and what happens then?
Project/branch/task: branch main, PLAN.md never states a max attempt count or what happens when retries run out.
ELI10: Retries must stop somewhere or a permanently broken job loops forever. When they stop, the job should land in the library's failed/dead-letter set where an operator can see it and re-enqueue it after the downstream is fixed. Without an alert, dead-lettered webhooks pile up silently and nobody notices until a customer asks where their events went.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Too few attempts drops events during a normal 10-minute outage. Too many with no alert means events sit dead for days unnoticed.
Recommendation: A because 10 attempts under the 5-min cap gives a ~19-minute retry window (covers typical outages), and the alert plus documented replay step is what makes 3am operable. Effort: A (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min), B (human: ~1 h / CC: ~2 min).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Net: bounded, observable failure with a replay path vs. a long silent tail.

options.label: 10 attempts, dead-letter + alert + documented replay (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Worst-case retry window ~19 min; exhausted jobs land in the library failed set and a metric/alert fires on dead-letter count > 0. ✅ Runbook line: re-enqueue from failed set after downstream recovers; idempotency key (R3) makes replay safe. ❌ One more metric and alert rule to wire and test.

options.label: 25 attempts, dead-letter, no alert
options.description: ✅ Survives longer outages (~2 h window) before giving up. ✅ No alerting work in this change. ❌ Silent failure: dead-lettered events are only found by someone looking; 2 h of hammering a downed service.

questions.question:
D8 — Extract the retry envelope into one shared module now, or leave 5 copies and refactor later?
Project/branch/task: branch main, PLAN.md:11-13 keeps the retry envelope copy-pasted across 5 worker files.
ELI10: After the decisions so far, the 'envelope' is a small set of things every worker needs identically: the backoff function, the constants (1 s base, 5 min cap, 10 attempts), the rule for which errors are retryable, and the attempt log line. Five copies means five places to drift: one worker gets a different cap, one forgets the idempotency header, one logs attempts differently so dashboards disagree. Extracting is one file plus five one-line imports.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Leaving copies invites silent config drift and quintuples the test surface. Extracting costs about ten minutes with CC and nothing later.
Recommendation: A because DRY is an explicit preference here, the extraction is mechanical, and the shared module is also where the retry state diagram comment lives. Effort: A (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min), B (human: 0 now, ~1 day later / CC: 0 now).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=3/10
Net: one source of truth for retry behavior vs. five that will drift.

options.label: Extract jobs/retry.ts now (recommended)
options.description: ✅ One module exports computeBackoff, retryOptions, isRetryable, logAttempt; all 5 workers import it, so R5-R7 values exist exactly once. ✅ Unit tests written once; per-worker tests shrink to 'uses retryOptions'. ❌ Touches all 5 worker files in this change (already touched by the rewrite anyway).

options.label: Leave 5 copies, refactor later
options.description: ✅ No cross-worker import to review; each worker stays self-contained. ✅ Matches the plan as written. ❌ Five copies of the cap/attempts constants and isRetryable rule drift independently; 'later' has no owner or trigger.

questions.question:
D9 — How deep should the webhook regression proof go: unit tests with mocks only, or unit tests plus one real-queue E2E?
Project/branch/task: branch main, proving the D4 webhook contract for the rewritten processWebhookJob().
ELI10: Unit tests with a mocked HTTP client and a mocked retry hook prove your code calls the hook correctly. They cannot prove the library actually re-dispatches the job with the same idempotency key after a delay, or that a dead-lettered job really shows up in the failed set. One end-to-end test runs the real library in test mode against a stub HTTP receiver and walks the four assertions for real. That is the integration point where mocking hides failures (API → queue → worker → receiver).
Stakes if we pick wrong: Mocks-only can pass while the real hook ignores your backoff function or drops the header on redispatch; you find out from a customer. E2E costs a slower test (seconds) and a stub receiver fixture.
Recommendation: A because this is exactly the flow the E2E decision matrix flags (3+ components, integration point, data-delivery guarantee) and CC writes the fixture in minutes. Effort: A (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min), B (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Net: proof the real queue honors the contract vs. proof your code asks it to.

options.label: Unit tests + one real-queue E2E (recommended)
options.description: ✅ E2E: enqueue -> stub receiver returns 503 then 200 -> asserts 2 POSTs, identical Idempotency-Key, delay came from computeBackoff (injected rng), then 4xx and exhaustion cases. ✅ Catches library-level surprises (hook signature, header loss on redispatch, failed-set behavior). ❌ Needs the library runnable in test mode (in-memory or ephemeral backend) and adds a few seconds to CI.

options.label: Unit tests with mocked HTTP and mocked hook only
options.description: ✅ Fast, deterministic, no external test backend needed. ✅ Still covers all four D4 assertions at the code level. ❌ Cannot detect a library that ignores the custom backoff or drops headers on retry; the contract is asserted, not demonstrated.

questions.question:
D10 — Cache the dependency graph across retries, measure first, or leave the recompute as-is?
Project/branch/task: branch main, PLAN.md:21-23 re-fetches the payload and recomputes the dependency graph on every retry attempt.
ELI10: When a job fails and retries, the plan reloads the whole payload from the database and rebuilds its dependency graph from scratch, up to 10 times per job now that max attempts is 10. If the graph is cheap this is noise. If it is not, every downstream outage turns into a database load spike on top of the retry storm. The catch: nobody has measured it, and the fixture repo has no code to inspect.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Caching an unchanging graph is safe but adds a serialized field and an invalidation rule for something that may cost 2 ms. Ignoring it means possibly 10x DB reads exactly during incidents.
Recommendation: B because the finding is medium confidence with zero measurements; a one-line timing log per attempt turns the next outage into data and costs almost nothing. Effort: A (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min), B (human: ~1 h / CC: ~5 min), C (0).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Net: optimize now on a guess vs. instrument now and optimize on evidence vs. ignore.

options.label: Cache graph on the job record, keyed by payload hash
options.description: ✅ Retries skip the payload fetch and graph build; invalidation by payload hash keeps it correct if the payload changes. ✅ Removes DB read amplification during the exact moments the system is already degraded. ❌ Adds job-data size and an invalidation path to test before anyone has shown the recompute is expensive.

options.label: Instrument first: log compute time + payload bytes per attempt (recommended)
options.description: ✅ One structured log line in logAttempt (graph_ms, payload_bytes) produces real numbers from the first incident. ✅ Decision to cache becomes a follow-up TODO with an explicit trigger (e.g. p95 graph_ms > 50 or payload > 100 KB). ❌ First real outage still pays the recompute cost; caching is deferred, not done.

options.label: Leave as-is, no instrumentation
options.description: ✅ Zero additional work in this change. ✅ Matches the plan as written. ❌ No data ever arrives, so the question stays a guess; retry-time DB load is invisible.

answers.D10 \u2014 Cache the dependency graph ac: Cache graph on the job record, keyed by payload hash

questions.question:
D11 — TODO: audit the other 4 workers' side effects for idempotency now that retries make them at-least-once?
Project/branch/task: branch main; retries are being enabled on all 5 workers, but only the webhook worker's delivery contract (R3) was decided.
ELI10: Turning on retries changes every worker from 'runs once' to 'may run more than once.' We settled how the webhook worker stays correct under that (stable idempotency key). The other four workers have side effects too (writes, emails, charges, whatever they do), and if any of them is not safe to re-run, a retry duplicates that effect. Nobody has looked.
What: Review each of the 4 non-webhook workers for non-idempotent side effects and add a guard (idempotency key, upsert, or exclusion from retries).
Why: Prevents duplicate side effects the moment retries ship.
Pros: Closes the gap R3 closed for webhooks; the shared jobs/retry.ts makes per-worker exclusion a one-line option.
Cons: Requires reading 4 handlers; may surface work that grows the change.
Context: Retries approved via library hook (D3), 10 attempts (D7). Start from each worker's handler and list its writes/external calls; classify each as idempotent, needs-key, or exclude-from-retry.
Depends on: T1 (jobs/retry.ts) for the exclusion mechanism. Effort: M (human: ~1 day / CC: ~30 min).
Stakes if we pick wrong: Skipping = duplicate side effects in whichever worker is not idempotent, discovered in production. Building now grows this PR.
Recommendation: C because enabling retries without knowing the handlers are safe to re-run is shipping the bug the framework is supposed to prevent; auditing 4 handlers is under an hour with CC.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: know every worker is retry-safe before retries ship vs. find out after.

options.label: Build it now in this PR instead of deferring (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Retries ship only after all 5 workers are known retry-safe; adds one task to the plan. ✅ Exclusion or keying reuses jobs/retry.ts already in scope. ❌ Widens the change if a handler turns out to need real idempotency work.

options.label: Add to TODOS.md
options.description: ✅ Captured with full context and priority so it is not lost. ✅ Keeps this change focused on the framework and the webhook path. ❌ Retries go live on 4 unaudited workers in the meantime.

options.label: Skip — not valuable enough
options.description: ✅ No extra work or tracking. ✅ Appropriate only if you already know all 4 handlers are idempotent. ❌ If that assumption is wrong, a retry duplicates a side effect with no record that the risk was considered.

answers.D11 \u2014 TODO: audit the other 4 worke: Build it now in this PR instead of deferring (recommended)
